analysis.one_liner: Limits brand-name drug makers to a single patent that can delay generic drug approval.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Sen. Durbin with one Republican cosponsor, has sat in the Senate health committee since July 2025 with no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: When a company wants to sell a cheaper copy of a brand-name drug, the brand company can sue over patent claims and automatically freeze the FDA's approval of the generic for 30 months. Today that freeze can be triggered repeatedly, once per patent, and brands often list many patents. This bill would let a brand company pick only one patent that can ever trigger the freeze, making it harder to stretch out a drug's monopoly years past what its patents legitimately cover — a practice known as 'evergreening.'
analysis.who_benefits: People who take prescription drugs, especially those paying full price before their insurance deductible, would get cheaper generic versions sooner. Generic drug makers also gain a clearer path to market.

how_it_helps.text: Under current law, a brand-name drug maker's patent lawsuit against a generic applicant triggers an automatic 30-month FDA approval stay, and because the stay can attach to any of the many patents listed for a drug, brands can stack or sequence delays that keep a cheaper copy off the market for years [S2].

The bill requires the brand company, at the time it lists patents with the FDA, to select a single 'covered patent,' and the selection cannot be changed, so only lawsuits over that one patent can trigger the 30-month stay for drugs approved after enactment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug companies, which would lose a tool for extending monopoly pricing past their core patents. Any reduction in extended monopoly revenue is the cost of the bill.

drawbacks.text: The bill addresses only the 30-month stay mechanism; other delay tactics, such as citizen petitions and patent settlements that keep generics out, are untouched, so it is a partial fix [S2].

A brand company holding several genuinely distinct patents loses the ability to enforce all of them through the stay process, which pharma companies could argue weakens protection for drugs with multiple legitimate inventions — the trade-off behind faster generics.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete: faster access to lower-cost generics for a drug class where delay tactics are well documented. The cost falls on brand-name manufacturers' extended monopoly revenue, which is precisely what the bill targets. The main limitation is that it narrows one delay pathway rather than all of them, so its real-world speed-up depends on brands not finding workarounds.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in July 2025 and referred to the Senate health committee, where it has sat with no hearings, no vote, and no floor action since.

narrative.text: Sen. Durbin introduced the REMEDY Act on July 31, 2025, joined by Sen. Cassidy as the bill's sole cosponsor, making it a two-senator bipartisan effort [S1].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions; the action history shows no further steps [S5].
The bill applies its one-patent rule only to drugs approved after enactment, leaving the existing process in place for drugs already on the market [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers are better off so far: with the bill stalled in committee, the current system allowing a 30-month FDA approval delay per patent remains intact.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the HELP Committee.

for.name: Sen. Bill Cassidy
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as its only additional Senate supporter.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has one Democrat (sponsor Durbin) and one Republican (cosponsor Cassidy); no one has opposed it on the record, and no vote has occurred.

industries.note: The bill limits them to one patent that can trigger the automatic 30-month FDA approval freeze, shrinking a key tool for extending monopoly pricing on drugs past their primary patents. Their gain comes from charging patients and insurers higher prices for longer.
With fewer patent-lawsuit delay freezes, generic companies can get FDA approval and reach the market sooner. Their interest in earlier entry runs alongside patients' interest in lower prices.

analysis.trajectory: With only two senators behind it, no committee action since referral, and no hearing scheduled, the bill is likely to die quietly in the HELP Committee this Congress, as do most bills at this stage.
